title: Effects of insulin and exenatide therapy on glycemic control and β-cell function in patients newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and severe hyperglycemia

citation.title: Effects of insulin and exenatide therapy on glycemic control and β-cell function in patients newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and severe hyperglycemia

printed_heading.text: Original Article J Chin Med Assoc www.ejcma.org   517 Effects of insulin and exenatide therapy on glycemic control and β-cell function in patients newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and severe hyperglycemia Tsung-Hui Wua,b , Chin-Sung Kuoa,b , Harn-Shen Chena,b, * a Division of Endocrinology and Metabolism, Department of Medicine, Taipei Veterans General Hospital, Taipei, Taiwan, ROC; b School of Medicine, College of Medicine, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, Taipei, Taiwan, ROC

what_it_measured.text: Compared with the exenatide group, the insulin group had better homeostasis model assessment of β-cell function index, insulinogenic index, and total insulin secretion during the OGTT.

Abstract Background: To assess the efficacy of short-term insulin therapy compared with exenatide therapy in glycemic control, remission rate, and β-cell function in patients newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes and severe hyperglycemia.

dose.text: In the exenatide (Byetta) therapy group, patients were instructed on exenatide injection techniques. The initial dose was 5 µg twice daily for 4 weeks, followed by 10 µg twice daily for 12 weeks.

route.text: If FPG concentrations were >200 mg/dL after 4 weeks of exenatide therapy, patients were withdrawn from the study and received an insulin injection as rescue therapy.
In the exenatide (Byetta) therapy group, patients were instructed on exenatide injection techniques.

endpoint.text: Outcomes The primary outcomes were the remission rate at 12 months after short-term intensive insulin therapy (randomization) and the duration of glycemic remission during the 18-month follow-up after randomization.The secondary outcomes were comparisons of changes in HbA1c levels, the proportion of participants who reached the therapy target (HbA1c <6.5% or <7.0% at 6 and 12 months after randomization), β-cell function, and insulin sensitivity calculated from the OGTT at 6 months. 2.8.

reported_results.text: The median time to relapse was 6.5 months in the insulin group and 5.0 months in the exenatide group (p = 0.685).

The mean HbA1c levels were similar between the insulin and exenatide groups at 6 months (6.74 ± 1.12% vs 6.88 ± 0.76%; p = 0.681) and 12 months after randomization (6.62 ± 0.69% vs 7.05 ± 0.72%; p = 0.119).
Results: We randomized 40 patients into the insulin group (n = 22) and the exenatide group (n = 18).

The median time to relapse was 6.5 months in the insulin group and 5.0 months in the exenatide group (p = 0.685). 3.4. β-Cell function and insulin resistance Table 2 shows the surrogate estimates of β-cell function and insulin resistance at the start of the study period and at the end of the intervention period in those who had OGTT data.
The insulin group was predominantly male and had a higher mean body mass index (BMI) than the exenatide group.The two treatment groups did not differ significantly in other clinical features. 3.2.
